claim: N-type (Cav2.2) calcium channels are present in the presynaptic nerve terminals of many neurons.
source: N-type (Cav2.2) calcium channels are present in the presynaptic nerve terminals of many neurons (Westenbroek et al., 1998), where they play a major role in synaptic transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Westenbroek et al., 1998.

claim: N-type channels in primary sensory neurons play a major role in pain/nociceptive signaling.
source: In particular, N-type channels in primary sensory neurons play a major role in pain/nociceptive signaling (Park and Luo, 2010; Hatakeyama et al., 2001; Saegusa et al., 2001; Sluka, 1997) and they are therefore an attractive target for inhibiting pain.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Park and Luo, 2010; Hatakeyama et al., 2001; Saegusa et al., 2001; Sluka, 1997.

claim: Ziconotide is a highly potent peptide blocker of N-type calcium channels used for intrathecal pain treatment.
source: In fact, one of the few new treatments for pain introduced in the last 50 years is intrathecal application of ziconotide, a highly potent peptide blocker of N-type calcium channels (Garber, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Garber, 2005.

claim: Ziconotide is a large peptide with three disulfide bridges that is expensive to synthesize and must be administered intrathecally.
source: While validating N-type calcium channels as a promising pharmacological target for treating pain, ziconotide has many practical drawbacks, as it is a large peptide with three disulfide bridges that is expensive to synthesize and must be administered intrathecally.
evidence: The claim is stated as a known fact about ziconotide's properties and limitations.

claim: Local anesthetics like lidocaine inhibit voltage-dependent sodium channels by binding tightly to open and inactivated states with relatively weak binding to the closed resting state.
source: The canonical small-molecule inhibitors of voltage-gated channels are local anesthetics like lidocaine, which inhibit voltage-dependent sodium channels by a mechanism that involves tight binding to open and inactivated states of the channel, with relatively weak binding to the closed resting state of the channel (Hille, 1977).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hille, 1977.

claim: QX-314 is ineffective in blocking neuronal sodium channels if applied externally.
source: QX-314 is ineffective in blocking neuronal sodium channels if applied externally (Frazier et al., 1970), apparently because it is too large to enter the outer mouth of the channel, but blocks effectively when applied to the internal (cytoplasmic) face of the channel, presumably because the inner mouth is larger.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Frazier et al., 1970.

claim: QX-314 blocks sodium channels effectively when applied to the internal (cytoplasmic) face of the channel.
source: QX-314 is ineffective in blocking neuronal sodium channels if applied externally (Frazier et al., 1970), apparently because it is too large to enter the outer mouth of the channel, but blocks effectively when applied to the internal (cytoplasmic) face of the channel, presumably because the inner mouth is larger.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Frazier et al., 1970.

claim: With intracellular application, QX-314 blocks sodium channels in a highly use-dependent manner because it enters channels only when the channels are open and is trapped inside channels when drug-occupied channels close.
source: With intracellular application, QX-314 blocks sodium channels in a highly use-dependent manner because it enters channels only when the channels are open and is trapped inside channels when drug-occupied channels close (Strichartz, 1973; Yeh, 1978; Cahalan and Almers, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Strichartz, 1973; Yeh, 1978; Cahalan and Almers, 1979.

claim: QX-314 can selectively block excitability of nociceptor neurons expressing channels like TRPV1 and TRPA1 by entering through their large pores.
source: The inability of QX-314 to inhibit from the outside of the cell can be exploited to selectively block excitability of nociceptor neurons expressing channels like TRPV1 and TRPA1, whose pores are large enough to pass the QX-314 cation into the cell, effectively silencing only these neurons and producing a selective elimination of pain or itch by blocking action potential conduction to the CNS (Binshtok et al., 2007; Roberson et al., 2011; Puopolo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Binshtok et al., 2007; Roberson et al., 2011; Puopolo et al., 2013.

claim: NNCB-2 is based on a scaffold of a family of molecules with blocking activity against N-type calcium channels described by Seko et al. (2001).
source: Its structure is based on a scaffold of a family of molecules with blocking activity against N-type calcium channels described by Seko et al. (2001), although it is not identical to any of the compounds they described.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Seko et al., 2001.

claim: 10 µM NNCB-2 inhibited calcium channel current by about 60%.
source: We found effective and dose-dependent inhibition, with 10 µM NNCB-2 inhibiting calcium channel current by about 60% and 100 µM NNCB-2 producing complete inhibition in about 30 s, when applied at a holding potential of −70 mV, near typical neuronal resting potentials.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 100 µM NNCB-2 produced complete inhibition of calcium channel current in about 30 s when applied at a holding potential of −70 mV.
source: We found effective and dose-dependent inhibition, with 10 µM NNCB-2 inhibiting calcium channel current by about 60% and 100 µM NNCB-2 producing complete inhibition in about 30 s, when applied at a holding potential of −70 mV, near typical neuronal resting potentials.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition by NNCB-2 was voltage-dependent, with weaker and slower inhibition at −100 mV compared to −70 mV.
source: Inhibition by NNCB-2 was voltage-dependent. Compared to inhibition when applied at −70 mV, application at a holding potential of −100 mV produced weaker inhibition that developed more slowly (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CNCB-2 inhibited Cav2.2 channels effectively with external application.
source: CNCB-2 inhibited Cav2.2 channels effectively with external application.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 100 µM CNCB-2 required about 3 min to produce complete inhibition of Cav2.2 channels.
source: Inhibition by CNCB-2 was slower than with the same concentration of the neutral compound, with 100 µM CNCB-2 requiring about 3 min to produce complete inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition by CNCB-2 was enhanced when channels were activated from a resting potential of −70 mV compared to −100 mV.
source: Similar to inhibition by NNCB-2, inhibition by CNCB-2 was enhanced when channels were activated from a resting potential of −70 mV compared to a resting potential of −100 mV, consistent with state-dependent binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both NNCB-2 and CNCB-2 were able to inhibit Cav2.2 channels effectively even in the absence of any channel opening.
source: We found that both NNCB-2 and CNCB-2 were able to inhibit effectively even in the absence of any channel opening.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Application of 100 µM CNCB-2 for 3 min in the absence of depolarizing pulses resulted in a decrease of current to 33 ± 5% of control (n = 4).
source: Application of 100 µM CNCB-2 for 3 min in the absence of stimulation resulted in a decrease of current to 33 ± 5% of control (n = 4, measured during the first depolarizing pulse after the 3 min application).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: A 3 min application of 100 µM CNCB-2 with depolarizing pulses reduced current to 5 ± 2% of control (n = 4).
source: However, the degree of inhibition produced by a 3 min application of 100 µM CNCB-2 in the absence of depolarizing pulses was less than the inhibition produced when depolarizing pulses were given during the application (50-millisecond steps from −70 to +10 mV delivered every 3 s, Figure 2), where a 3 min application reduced current to 5 ± 2% of control (n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size, referencing Figure 2.

claim: Recovery from CNCB-2 inhibition was much slower than from NNCB-2 when the agent was removed.
source: A major difference between the inhibition produced by the cationic and neutral compounds was that recovery from CNCB-2 inhibition was much slower than from NNCB-2 when the agent was removed (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: With 3 min of wash-out after exposure to 100 µM NNCB-2, current recovered from −1 ± 11% to 81 ± 10% (n = 4) of the initial control value.
source: With 3 min of wash-out after exposure to 100 µM NNCB-2, current recovered from −1 ± 11% to 81 ± 10% (n = 4) of the initial control value before compound was applied.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: With 3 min of wash-out after exposure to 100 µM CNCB-2, current recovered from 11 ± 6% to 28 ± 4% (n = 4).
source: However, with 3 min of wash-out after exposure to 100 µM CNCB-2, current recovered much less, from 11 ± 6% to 28 ± 4% (n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: Inhibition by internal CNCB-2 developed more slowly than with external application.
source: However, inhibition by internal CNCB-2 developed more slowly than with external application.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: With 300 µM CNCB-2 applied internally, current was reduced to 20% of the initial control value after 114 s.
source: With 300 µM CNCB-2 applied internally, current was reduced to 20% of the initial control value after 114 s, while the same reduction took only 27 s with external application of 300 µM CNCB-2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements.

claim: The same reduction in current took only 27 s with external application of 300 µM CNCB-2.
source: With 300 µM CNCB-2 applied internally, current was reduced to 20% of the initial control value after 114 s, while the same reduction took only 27 s with external application of 300 µM CNCB-2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements.

claim: Approximately 80–90% of the overall voltage-dependent calcium current in mouse superior cervical ganglion (SCG) sympathetic neurons is carried by N-type calcium channels.
source: To examine whether CNCB-2 applied externally can inhibit native N-type calcium channels in neurons as well as cloned N-type channels expressed in HEK cells, we tested its effects on calcium channels in mouse superior cervical ganglion (SCG) sympathetic neurons, a neuronal type in which ~ 80–90% of the overall voltage-dependent calcium current is carried by N-type calcium channels (Regan et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Regan et al., 1991.

claim: Externally applied CNCB-2 was effective in inhibiting calcium channel current in SCG neurons, with an IC50 near 3 µM.
source: Externally applied CNCB-2 was effective in inhibiting calcium channel current in SCG neurons, with an IC50 near 3 µM (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CNCB-2 also inhibits sodium channels with external application, acting even more potently on sodium channels than on N-type calcium channels.
source: Surprisingly, however, we found that CNCB-2 also inhibits sodium channels with external application, acting even more potently on sodium channels than on N-type calcium channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: With a holding potential of −70 mV and 10-msec depolarizing steps to 0 mV delivered every 5 s, 3 µM CNCB-2 inhibited sodium current to 31 ± 5% of control with application for 10 min (n = 5).
source: With a holding potential of −70 mV and 10-msec depolarizing steps to 0 mV delivered every 5 s, 3 µM CNCB-2 inhibited sodium current to 31 ± 5% of control with application for 10 min (n = 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: Inhibition of Nav1.7 channels by CNCB-2 was voltage-dependent, with more potent inhibition from more depolarized holding potentials.
source: Inhibition of Nav1.7 channels by CNCB-2 was voltage-dependent, with more potent inhibition from more depolarized holding potentials, in a manner suggesting higher-affinity binding to inactivated states of the sodium channel.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 3 µM CNCB-2 produced equal inhibition at holding voltages of −120 mV and −100 mV (to 67 ± 5% of control at −120 mV and to 67 ± 4% of control at −100 mV).
source: Using a protocol in which various holding voltages were established for 2 s in a staircase-like manner, 3 µM CNCB-2 produced equal inhibition at holding voltages of −120 mV and −100 mV (to 67 ± 5% of control at −120 mV and to 67 ± 4% of control at −100 mV), where channels are in the resting state, but much more effective inhibition at more depolarized voltages where more channels are in inactivated states, inhibiting to 12 ± 4% of control from a holding potential of −60 mV where ~ 55% of channels are in the inactivated state under control conditions (n = 5 for all measurements).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: 3 µM CNCB-2 inhibited Nav1.7 channels to 12 ± 4% of control from a holding potential of −60 mV where ~ 55% of channels are in the inactivated state under control conditions (n = 5).
source: Using a protocol in which various holding voltages were established for 2 s in a staircase-like manner, 3 µM CNCB-2 produced equal inhibition at holding voltages of −120 mV and −100 mV (to 67 ± 5% of control at −120 mV and to 67 ± 4% of control at −100 mV), where channels are in the resting state, but much more effective inhibition at more depolarized voltages where more channels are in inactivated states, inhibiting to 12 ± 4% of control from a holding potential of −60 mV where ~ 55% of channels are in the inactivated state under control conditions (n = 5 for all measurements).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: The estimated binding affinity of CNCB-2 to resting Nav1.7 channels is KR = 5.6 µM.
source: Making this calculation (and using the inhibition at −120 mV where channels are all in the resting state to estimate KR) results in estimates of KR = 5.6 µM and KI = 0.71 µM.
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations based on experimental data.

claim: The estimated binding affinity of CNCB-2 to inactivated Nav1.7 channels is KI = 0.71 µM.
source: Making this calculation (and using the inhibition at −120 mV where channels are all in the resting state to estimate KR) results in estimates of KR = 5.6 µM and KI = 0.71 µM.
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations based on experimental data.

claim: The estimated binding affinity of lidocaine to resting sodium channels is KR = 440 µM.
source: This can be compared to the estimates of KR = 440 µM and KI = 10 µM for lidocaine binding to sodium channels (Bean et al., 1983), implying much tighter binding of CNCB-2 than lidocaine to both resting and inactivated states of the channel.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bean et al., 1983.

claim: The estimated binding affinity of lidocaine to inactivated sodium channels is KI = 10 µM.
source: This can be compared to the estimates of KR = 440 µM and KI = 10 µM for lidocaine binding to sodium channels (Bean et al., 1983), implying much tighter binding of CNCB-2 than lidocaine to both resting and inactivated states of the channel.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bean et al., 1983.

claim: CNCB-2 binds much more tightly than lidocaine to both resting and inactivated states of sodium channels.
source: This can be compared to the estimates of KR = 440 µM and KI = 10 µM for lidocaine binding to sodium channels (Bean et al., 1983), implying much tighter binding of CNCB-2 than lidocaine to both resting and inactivated states of the channel.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of binding constants.

claim: Inhibition of Nav1.7 channels by CNCB-2 was strongly use-dependent.
source: Inhibition of Nav1.7 channels by CNCB-2 was strongly-use-dependent.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both the rate of inhibition and the degree of inhibition by CNCB-2 were greater with more rapid stimulation.
source: Both the rate of inhibition and the degree of inhibition were greater with more rapid stimulation (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The use-dependent inhibition by CNCB-2 was more potent than that by lidocaine or even by bupivacaine.
source: The use-dependent inhibition by CNCB-2 was more potent than that by lidocaine or even by bupivacaine, the most potent of local anesthetics commonly used clinically (Becker and Reed, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Becker and Reed, 2012.

claim: In the absence of drug, 2 min of stimulation at 10 Hz reduced current to 77 ± 3% (n = 12).
source: In the absence of drug, 2 min of stimulation at 10 Hz reduced current to 77 ± 3% (n = 12), reflecting accumulation into a slow inactivated state from which current recovered quickly on a return to 0.1 Hz stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: With 3 µM CNCB-2, current during the 10 Hz stimulation was reduced to 14 ± 8% of control (n = 5).
source: With 3 µM CNCB-2, current during the 10 Hz stimulation was reduced to 14 ± 8% of control (n = 5), with only slow and partial recovery of current when stimulation was returned to 0.1 Hz.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: 30 µM lidocaine reduced current to 57 ± 7% of control during 10 Hz stimulation (n = 6).
source: The use-dependent reduction by 3 µM CNCB-2 was more pronounced than by 30 µM lidocaine (reduction to 57 ± 7% of control, n = 6) and similar to 10 µM bupivacaine (reduction to 22 ± 4%, n = 5), with much slower reversal than either lidocaine or bupivacaine when returning to 0.1 Hz stimulation (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size, shown in Figure 6.

claim: 10 µM bupivacaine reduced current to 22 ± 4% of control during 10 Hz stimulation (n = 5).
source: The use-dependent reduction by 3 µM CNCB-2 was more pronounced than by 30 µM lidocaine (reduction to 57 ± 7% of control, n = 6) and similar to 10 µM bupivacaine (reduction to 22 ± 4%, n = 5), with much slower reversal than either lidocaine or bupivacaine when returning to 0.1 Hz stimulation (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size, shown in Figure 6.

claim: CNCB-2 applied internally at 3 µM produced very little inhibition of Nav1.7 channels even with 2–3 series of 2 min stimulation at 10 Hz.
source: In three cells, CNCB-2 applied internally at 3 µM produced very little inhibition even with 2–3 series of 2 min stimulation at 10 Hz.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from three cells.

claim: When 3 µM CNCB-2 was applied externally after internal application, it immediately produced inhibition during the stimulation at 10 Hz.
source: However, when 3 µM CNCB-2 was then applied externally, it immediately produced inhibition during the stimulation at 10 Hz, exactly as when external 3 µM CNCB-2 was applied in the absence of internal CNCB-2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CNCB-2 accesses its binding sites on both Nav1.7 and Cav2.2 channels most easily from the external surface of the membrane.
source: Thus, it appears that CNCB-2 accesses its binding sites on both Nav1.7 and Cav2.2 channels most easily from the external surface of the membrane.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations of differential effects with internal vs external application.

claim: CNCB-2 potently inhibits action potential firing in small diameter DRG neurons.
source: We found that CNCB-2 potently inhibits action potential firing in these neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Application of CNCB-2 produced a depolarization of the resting potential of DRG neurons from −76 ± 2 mV in control to −62 ± 3 mV (n = 5) after application of 3 µM CNCB-2.
source: In addition to dramatically depressing action potential firing, application of CNCB-2 produced a depolarization of the resting potential of the neurons, from −76 ± 2 mV in control to −62 ± 3 mV (n = 5) after application of 3 µM CNCB-2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: The depolarization of the resting potential by CNCB-2 was never enough to stimulate firing of the neurons.
source: This depolarization of the resting potential was never enough to stimulate firing of the neurons (which had an average threshold voltage of −32 ± 1 mV, n = 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: The number of action potentials evoked by a 1 s 80 pA current injection was reduced from 18 ± 8 in control to 0.6 ± 0.2 after application of 3 µM CNCB-2 (n = 5) when resting potential was adjusted.
source: On average, the number of action potentials evoked by a 1 s 80 pA current injection was reduced from 18 ± 8 in control to 0.6 ± 0.2 after application of 3 µM CNCB-2 (n = 5), similar to the depression of firing in an earlier series in which resting potential was not adjusted (13 ± 2 spikes in control to 2 ± 1 after application of 3 µM CNCB-2, n = 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: CNCB-2 dramatically depressed the peak of the action potential from +30 ± 3 mV in control to −2 ± 2 mV in 3 µM CNCB-2 (n = 4, holding potential adjusted in CNCB-2).
source: In addition to the reduction in the number of action potentials evoked by current injection, CNCB-2 dramatically depressed the peak of the action potential (from +30 ± 3 mV in control to −2 ± 2 mV in 3 µM CNCB-2, n = 4, holding potential adjusted in CNCB-2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: The action potential in small diameter nociceptive DRG neurons is mediated by a combination of TTX-sensitive sodium current and TTX-resistant sodium current, carried mainly by Nav1.8 channels.
source: The action potential in small diameter nociceptive DRG neurons is mediated by a combination of TTX-sensitive sodium current, which helps initiate the action potential, and TTX-resistant sodium current, carried mainly by Nav1.8 channels, which generally provides the majority of total sodium current during the action potential (Renganathan et al., 2001; Blair and Bean, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Renganathan et al., 2001; Blair and Bean, 2002.

claim: CNCB-2 effectively inhibited both TTX-sensitive and TTX-resistant components of sodium current in DRG neurons.
source: We tested this in voltage clamp experiments and found that CNCB-2 effectively inhibited both TTX-sensitive and TTX-resistant components of sodium current in DRG neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 30 µM CNCB-2 inhibited overall sodium current in small DRG neurons nearly completely (reduction to 4 ± 1% of control, n = 10, CNCB-2 applied for 2.5–5 min).
source: In a first series of experiments, we found that 30 µM CNCB-2 inhibited overall sodium current in small DRG neurons nearly completely (reduction to 4 ± 1% of control, n = 10, CNCB-2 applied for 2.5–5 min).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: 3 µM CNCB-2 inhibited TTX-resistant sodium current to 23 ± 6% of control (n = 6).
source: At 3 µM, CNCB-2 inhibited TTX-resistant sodium current to 23 ± 6% of control (n = 6) and 10 µM CNCB-2 inhibited TTX-resistant sodium current to 10 ± 3% of control (n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: 10 µM CNCB-2 inhibited TTX-resistant sodium current to 10 ± 3% of control (n = 4).
source: At 3 µM, CNCB-2 inhibited TTX-resistant sodium current to 23 ± 6% of control (n = 6) and 10 µM CNCB-2 inhibited TTX-resistant sodium current to 10 ± 3% of control (n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size.

claim: A single injection of 10 μL of either 15 mM or 30 mM CNCB-2 directly adjacent to the incision resulted in a reduction of mechanical sensitivity that lasted for at least 8 hr in the paw incision model.
source: Twenty-four hours after the incision, a single injection of 10 μL of either 15 mM or 30 mM CNCB-2 directly adjacent to the incision resulted in a reduction of mechanical sensitivity that lasted for at least 8 hr (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: 30 mM bupivacaine produced no remaining analgesic effect 1 hr after injection in the paw incision model.
source: In contrast, 30 mM bupivacaine produced no remaining analgesic effect 1 hr after injection, in marked contrast to the long-lasting effects of CNCB-2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bupivacaine injected alone without norepinephrine had effects lasting only 25 min in a previous study.
source: The short duration of action of bupivacaine in this model is consistent with a previous study in which bupivacaine injected alone without norepinephrine (generally co-applied with bupivacaine in clinical settings to produce vasoconstriction and thereby slow washout of bupivacaine by blood flow) had effects lasting only 25 min (Grant et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grant et al., 1997.

claim: CNCB-2 was exceptionally effective in the zymosan model of inflammatory pain, increasing the 50% withdrawal threshold from 0.20 ± 0.08 grams to 3.6 ± 0.2 grams (n = 5).
source: CNCB-2 was exceptionally effective in this model (Figure 9B), increasing the 50% withdrawal threshold from 0.20 ± 0.08 grams to 3.6 ± 0.2 grams (n = 5) of pressure.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with specific measurements and sample size, shown in Figure 9B.

claim: CNCB-2 produced effective analgesia when injected in paws of naïve mice, with analgesia lasting for at least 4 hr.
source: CNCB-2 produced effective analgesia when injected in paws of naïve mice, with analgesia lasting for at least 4 hr (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Calcium entry through N-type calcium channels triggers release of neuropeptides from primary sensory neurons by activating vesicular release.
source: Calcium entry through N-type calcium channels triggers release of neuropeptides from primary sensory neurons by activating vesicular release (Holz et al., 1988; Evans et al., 1996; Chi et al., 2009; Amrutkar et al., 2011; Takasusuki and Yaksh, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Holz et al., 1988; Evans et al., 1996; Chi et al., 2009; Amrutkar et al., 2011; Takasusuki and Yaksh, 2011.

claim: Both NNCB-2 and CNCB-2 were able to reduce CGRP release from cultured DRG neurons, with greater efficacy of inhibition by CNCB-2.
source: Studying release of CGRP from cultured DRG neurons induced by depolarization (exposure to 50 mM KCl), we found that both NNCB-2 and CNCB-2 were able to reduce CGRP release, with greater efficacy of inhibition by CNCB-2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Exposure to 30 µM CNCB-2 dramatically reduced lung inflammation compared to exposure to vehicle in the ovalbumin-based model of allergic airway disease.
source: Exposure to 30 µM CNCB-2 dramatically reduced lung inflammation compared to exposure to vehicle, with a reduction of CD3+ cells (lymphocytes) to ~20% of the levels with no CNCB-2 exposure and reductions to 25–35% for the other inflammation-associated immune cell types tested (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The effects of 100 µM NNCB-2 were quantitatively very similar to those of 30 µM CNCB-2 in the allergic airway inflammation model.
source: In keeping with a greater efficacy of CNCB-2 in this model, the effects of 100 µM NNCB-2 were quantitatively very similar to those of 30 µM CNCB-2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Topical administration of CNCB-2 is an effective way to inhibit the neurogenic component of allergic inflammation in a long-lasting manner.
source: We conclude that topical administration of CNCB-2 is an effective way to inhibit the neurogenic component of allergic inflammation in a long-lasting manner.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on allergic airway inflammation.

claim: The charged version of the N-type calcium channel inhibitor was more effective in inhibiting N-type calcium channels with external than with internal application.
source: We had two major surprises in the course of the work: first, that the charged version of the N-type calcium channel inhibitor was more effective in inhibiting N-type calcium channels with external than with internal application, in striking contrast to the charged lidocaine derivative QX-314, which acts only with intracellular application and has no effect when applied extracellularly (Frazier et al., 1970; Binshtok et al., 2007) and second, that the molecule is also a highly effective inhibitor of sodium channels when applied externally.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and citations to Frazier et al., 1970; Binshtok et al., 2007.

claim: CNCB-2 is a highly effective inhibitor of sodium channels when applied externally.
source: We had two major surprises in the course of the work: first, that the charged version of the N-type calcium channel inhibitor was more effective in inhibiting N-type calcium channels with external than with internal application, in striking contrast to the charged lidocaine derivative QX-314, which acts only with intracellular application and has no effect when applied extracellularly (Frazier et al., 1970; Binshtok et al., 2007) and second, that the molecule is also a highly effective inhibitor of sodium channels when applied externally.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Preferential binding to inactivated states of the channel is characteristic of many non-permanently charged small molecule inhibitors of both sodium and calcium channels.
source: Preferential binding to inactivated states of the channel is characteristic of many non-permanently charged small molecule inhibitors of both sodium and calcium channels (Lenkey et al., 2010; Lenkey et al., 2011; Swensen et al., 2012): Kuryshev et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lenkey et al., 2010; Lenkey et al., 2011; Swensen et al., 2012; Kuryshev et al., 2014.

claim: QX-314 entry and exit appear to occur only when the sodium channel is actually open.
source: Interestingly, however, QX-314 inhibition of sodium channels is qualitatively different from that of uncharged molecules in that QX-314 entry and exit appear to occur only when the channel is actually open (Cahalan and Almers, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cahalan and Almers, 1979.

claim: CNCB-2, like lidocaine, can clearly bind to inactivated channels in the absence of any significant channel opening.
source: In contrast, CNCB-2, like lidocaine, can clearly bind to inactivated channels in the absence of any significant channel opening.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Recent molecular modeling suggests that the charged (protonated) form of lidocaine binds in the pore domain of sodium channels, with the cationic region of the molecule near the selectivity filter.
source: Recent molecular modeling enabled by cryo-EM structures of eukaryotic sodium channels suggests that the charged (protonated) form of lidocaine binds in the pore domain, with the cationic region of the molecule near the selectivity filter, partially displacing sodium ions in the selectivity filter (Buyan et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buyan et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2019.

claim: Modeling shows that the binding site for lidocaine in sodium channels can accommodate two lidocaine molecules.
source: Modeling shows that the binding site for lidocaine in sodium channels can accommodate two lidocaine molecules (Nguyen et al., 2019), suggesting that the same intra-pore binding site could also accommodate the larger CNCB-2 molecule (MW 435 Daltons vs 234 Daltons for lidocaine).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2019.

claim: Sodium channel inhibition by external application has been reported for several other cationic small molecules, notably cationic derivatives of amitriptyline and duloxetine.
source: Sodium channel inhibition by external application has been reported for several other cationic small molecules, notably cationic derivatives of amitriptyline and duloxetine (Gerner et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2016), tricyclic molecules introduced clinically as antidepressants that have become first-line treatments for neuropathic pain (Dworkin et al., 2010) where they may act in part by inhibition of sodium channels (Dick et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gerner et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2016; Dworkin et al., 2010; Dick et al., 2007.

claim: The interaction of CNCB-2 with sodium channels (estimated KR of 5.6 µM and KI of 0.71 µM) is far more potent than for N-methyl-duloxetine (estimated KR of 138 µM and KI of 2.8 µM).
source: However, the interaction of CNCB-2 with sodium channels (estimated KR of 5.6 µM and KI of 0.71 µM) is far more potent than for N-methyl-duloxetine (estimated KR of 138 µM and KI of 2.8 µM), especially for interacting with the resting state of the channel.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of binding constants from experimental data.

claim: A charged derivative of the benzothiazepine drug diltiazem behaves much like the QX-314 mediated inhibition of sodium channels, with little effect with external application but able to inhibit with intracellular application in a strongly use-dependent manner.
source: A charged derivative of the benzothiazepine drug diltiazem behaves much like the QX-314 mediated inhibition of sodium channels, with little effect with external application but able to inhibit with intracellular application in a strongly use-dependent manner, as if the compound can enter channels from the inside and only when channels are open (Shabbir et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shabbir et al., 2011.

claim: Charged versions of the dihydropyridine class of calcium channel inhibitors produce inhibition only with external application and have no effect when applied inside the cell.
source: In contrast, however, charged versions of the dihydropyridine class of calcium channel inhibitors have the opposite behavior, producing inhibition only with external application and having no effect when applied inside the cell (Kass et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kass et al., 1991.

claim: The ability to non-selectively inhibit a wide range of sodium channels may be advantageous for a charged compound administered locally because nociceptive neurons express a range of sodium channels.
source: However, the ability to non-selectively inhibit a wide range of sodium channels may actually be advantageous for a charged compound administered locally, because nociceptive neurons express a range of sodium channels (Zheng et al., 2019) and inhibiting only one of them may not effectively block excitability.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2019 and logical inference.

claim: Systemic exposure to CNCB-2 is likely to be very low, since the charged molecule is unlikely to penetrate well through tissue into the blood stream.
source: However, systemic exposure is likely to be very low, since the charged molecule is unlikely to penetrate well through tissue into the blood stream, which should minimize unwanted effects in tissues away from the site of application, including the heart and brain, unlike local application of anesthetics like lidocaine and bupivacaine.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the charged nature of the molecule.

claim: Externally applied CNCB-2 inhibits sodium channels more potently than bupivacaine.
source: It is remarkable that externally applied CNCB-2 inhibits sodium channels more potently than bupivacaine, one of the most potent local anesthetics.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many kinds of inflammation involve a 'vicious cycle' of interactions between immune cells and nociceptor sensory neuron endings.
source: Many kinds of inflammation involve a 'vicious cycle' of interactions between immune cells and nociceptor sensory neuron endings, in which inflammatory mediators from immune cells stimulate the neurons to release neuropeptides like CGRP, substance P, and VIP, which enhance local immune influx by producing vasodilation and increasing capillary permeability and can directly activate immune cells to release more cytokines (Chiu et al., 2012; Foster et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2014; Luger, 2002; Nijhuis et al., 2010; Riol-Blanco et al., 2014; Talbot et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chiu et al., 2012; Foster et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2014; Luger, 2002; Nijhuis et al., 2010; Riol-Blanco et al., 2014; Talbot et al., 2015.

claim: N-type (Cav2.2) calcium channels mediate the neuronal release of neuropeptides and are highly expressed in peptidergic primary sensory neurons involved in neurogenic inflammation.
source: In particular, N-type (Cav2.2) calcium channels mediate the neuronal release of neuropeptides and are found to be highly expressed in peptidergic primary sensory neurons involved in neurogenic inflammation (Amrutkar et al., 2011; Dunlap et al., 1989; Holz et al., 1988; Takasusuki and Yaksh, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Amrutkar et al., 2011; Dunlap et al., 1989; Holz et al., 1988; Takasusuki and Yaksh, 2011.

claim: Inhibiting N-type channels with CNCB-2 constitutes a novel approach to reducing inflammation by inhibiting release of neuropeptides.
source: Inhibiting N-type channels with CNCB-2 constitutes a novel approach to reducing inflammation by inhibiting release of neuropeptides.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and mechanism of action.

claim: CNCB-2 is more effective at 30 μM than 100 μM QX-314 in reducing allergic airway inflammation.
source: CNCB-2 is more effective at 30 μM (Figure 10) than 100 μM QX-314 (Talbot et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10 and a citation to Talbot et al., 2015.

claim: CNCB-2 can act even before inflammation is present, potentially preventing its establishment.
source: Unlike QX-314 which will only enter cells in the presence of activated large pore channels, a feature of active inflammation, CNCB-2 can act even before inflammation is present, potentially preventing its establishment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mechanism of action of CNCB-2 compared to QX-314.

claim: The ability of combined calcium and sodium channel inhibition to reduce allergic airway inflammation is consistent with extensive evidence of a strong involvement of neuropeptide release in this form of inflammation.
source: The ability of combined calcium and sodium channel inhibition to reduce allergic airway inflammation is consistent with extensive evidence of a strong involvement of neuropeptide release in this form of inflammation (Caceres et al., 2009; Patterson et al., 2007; Talbot et al., 2015; Wallrapp et al., 2017) and with the effect of sodium channel blockade with QX-314 in this model (Talbot et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Caceres et al., 2009; Patterson et al., 2007; Talbot et al., 2015; Wallrapp et al., 2017.

claim: Making cationic versions of N-type calcium channel blocker molecules that have external blocking activity on calcium and sodium channels may be a new route to identifying new powerful agents for treating pain and inflammatory conditions with a neurogenic component.
source: Our results suggest that making cationic versions of such molecules that have external blocking activity on calcium and sodium channels may be an unexpected new route to identifying new powerful agents well-suited for both treating pain from injury and surgery and inflammatory conditions with a neurogenic component.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.
